newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.N. rights envoy worried about Bosnia refugeeS.
newsitem.headline: U.N. rights envoy worried about Bosnia refugeeS.

text.p: The U.N.'s top human rights envoy expressed strong concerns on Friday over an agreement between international mediators and Moslems trying to resettle a village on Bosnian Serb-held territory.

In a letter to the commander of NATO forces in Bosnia, obtained by Reuters, Special Human Rights Rapporteur Elisabeth Rehn said she felt the human rights of the refugees "are not being adequately respected".

"My opinion is that international handling of this crisis has profound implications for the implementation of voluntary returns on a country-wide basis," Rehn said in the letter to Admiral Joseph Lopez.

International mediators struck an agreement on Thursday with Moslem refugees in the village of Jusici, under Serb control in northeast Bosnia, to withraw and return with proper paperwork in three days time.
An international commission has also been set up to process applications of those who want to return to Jusici.
More than 100 Moslem men, claiming to be former residents of the village, crossed former frontlines two weeks ago to reclaim their homes.

Some carried weapons, in clear violation of the Dayton accord banning weapons inside the so-called "Zone of Separation" (ZOS), a two-km wide strip of demilitarised land dividing the former warring factions.
Relief workers opposed the plan, saying that refugees should be allowed to go back to their homes without having to apply, as promised in Bosnia's peace accord.
But the ZOS is a highly sensitive area and NATO, charged with making sure no weapons or troops are inside it, welcomed the Jusici agreement.

"We consider this is not only a fresh start for citizens of Jusici, but a fresh start for the entire effort of trying to get refugees to return to the zone of separation," NATO spokesman Major Simon Haselock said.
But others, like Rehn, feared it might become a model not only for the ZOS but for the rest of the country, and could seriously slow the process of returns.
"The right to voluntary return clearly is established both in international laws and in Bosnia's peace agreement," Rehn said, urging Lopez to ensure NATO respects that right.
Kris Janowski, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), agreed the Jusici agreement should not set a precedent.
"We accepted the temporary removal of Jusici villagers just because of the complicated security situation. We would not be happy if it became a model for other areas," he said.
"The right of refugees to return is enshrined in the Dayton peace accord. That is wholly their right."

The Dayton peace accord, signed last December, ended 43 months of fighting and guaranteed freedom of movement and right to return to all refugees. But only a few hundred people have dared venture across former frontlines to their pre-war homes.
